title: Linear Equations and Integrating Factors
short: Multiply by e^(∫p dt) so the left side becomes a product's derivative.
trouble: Students use the integrating factor before putting the equation in standard form, or multiply only the left side.

blocks.html: Separable equations can be solved by moving all the $y$'s to one side. An equation like $y' + 2y = 4$ also separates, but $y' + 2y = e^{t}$ does not. Linear first-order equations need one new idea: multiply by a well-chosen function so that the left side becomes the derivative of a product.

Write the equation in standard form $y' + p(t)y = g(t)$. Multiply both sides by the integrating factor $\mu(t) = e^{\int p(t)\,dt}$. The left side becomes $(\mu y)'$, so $$\mu y = \int \mu g\,dt + C,$$ $$y = \frac{1}{\mu}\left(\int \mu g\,dt + C\right).$$

We want $\mu y' + \mu p y$ to equal $(\mu y)' = \mu y' + \mu' y$. Comparing the two, we need $\mu' = p\mu$, a separable equation whose solution is $\mu = e^{\int p\,dt}$. Any antiderivative of $p$ works, because a different constant only multiplies $\mu$ by a constant, which cancels at the end.

items: Divide by the coefficient of $y'$ to reach standard form, and read off $p(t)$.
Multiply both sides by $\mu$ and write the left side as $(\mu y)'$.
Integrate both sides (with $+C$), divide by $\mu$, then use the initial condition.

blocks.title: Constant coefficients
blocks.a: $y = 2 + 3e^{-2t}$. The 2 is the equilibrium; the $3e^{-2t}$ part dies out.

blocks.title: When the forcing matches the decay
blocks.a: $y = (t - 1)e^{t}$. The integral produced a factor $t$, a first sign of resonance.

blocks.html: Two slips are common. (1) Computing $\mu$ from the coefficient of $y$ before dividing by the coefficient of $y'$: for $ty' + 2y = 6t$, using $p = 2$ instead of $\frac{2}{t}$. (2) Multiplying only the left side by $\mu$. Check your $\mu$: after multiplying, the left side must be exactly $(\mu y)'$; expand it and compare.

blocks.name: slopefield
blocks.cap: Solutions of $y' = 4 - 2y$. Every curve approaches the equilibrium $y = 2$; the general solution $2 + Ce^{-2t}$ shows why. The blue curve starts at $(0, 5)$.

blocks.html: The general solution of a linear equation always has the shape particular solution + $C$ times $e^{-\int p\,dt}$. The second part solves $y' + py = 0$. This split returns, in a bigger form, for second-order equations.
